The periodization of history into discrete eras (Antiquity, Medieval, Early Modern, and so forth) is a taxonomic convenience rather than a reflection of how historical change actually operates. Transitions between periods are invariably gradual, contested, and recognizable only in retrospect. The "fall" of Rome, conventionally dated to 476 CE (when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus), was scarcely noted by contemporaries, most of whom experienced continuity rather than rupture.

Primary source analysis requires careful attention to the distinction between what a document says and what it reveals. A medieval charter granting land to a monastery tells us not only about property transfer but also (implicitly) about literacy rates, legal conventions, and the relationship between ecclesiastical and secular authority. The historian's task is to read both the text and its silences.

Quantitative methods have become increasingly prominent in historical scholarship since the 1960s (the so-called "cliometric revolution"). Demographic reconstruction, price series analysis, and network modeling now complement traditional narrative approaches. These methods are particularly valuable for studying populations that left few written records, though they carry their own epistemological limitations (notably, the assumption that surviving data constitute a representative sample).
